content_html:
Hopfield Attractor-Network Memory

Hopfield networks are fully recurrent neural networks that store memories as stable activity patterns (attractors). From a partial or noisy cue, the network’s dynamics settle into the nearest attractor, enabling content‑addressable, error‑correcting retrieval.

Why it matters

  • Energy function guarantees convergence to a stable state.
  • Capacity ≈ 0.14 × N random patterns for N binary units (dense connectivity; beyond this, interference and spurious attractors grow).
  • Separation ↔ completion: Dentate gyrus helps separate similar inputs; CA3 completes from partial cues.
  • Associative recall: recall emerges from dynamics, not lookup.
  • Robustness: noise is cleaned as the state “falls” into an energy well.
  • Biological analogy: hippocampal CA3 recurrent circuitry supports pattern completion for episodic retrieval.

Energy landscape

Each valley is an attractor (stored memory). The system’s state rolls “downhill” into the nearest valley, cleaning noise and completing the pattern.

How it works

  1. Encoding (Hebbian learning): co‑active units strengthen symmetric connections. This sculpts an energy surface with minima at the stored patterns.
  2. Retrieval: present a partial/noisy cue → iterate updates → the state relaxes to the nearest minimum (attractor), reconstructing the full pattern.
  3. Limits and trade‑offs: with dense random binary patterns, reliable capacity ≈ 0.138N–0.144N; sparse coding and diluted connectivity can increase effective capacity and reduce spurious states.

Analogy to biology

Hippocampal dentate gyrus emphasizes pattern separation (decorrelating similar inputs), while recurrent CA3 emphasizes pattern completion (retrieving from fragments) — a division of labor that supports episodic memory.
